ls.b_connect.title: Connecting
ls.b_connect.intro:
You win when your stones form an unbroken chain between your two edges. Stones on touching cells are connected.

Before every move, check whether one stone would complete your chain. Corner cells belong to both edges.
ls.b_connect.goal: Connect your two edges with one stone.
ls.b_connect.hint: Look along your chain for the one gap left. The dashed rings mark its area.
ls.b_connect.ng: {x} does not connect yet. {m} joins your edges.
ls.b_block.title: Blocking
ls.b_block.intro:
When the opponent needs only one more stone, you must take that cell yourself. Your stone blocks the chain.

Turn on "Show cells that connect at once" in the new-game dialog to see such cells during games.
ls.b_block.hint: Find the cell where the opponent would connect. The dashed rings mark its area.
ls.b_block.ng: After {x} the opponent connects. Only {m} blocks.
ls.b_bridge.title: Two threats at once
ls.b_bridge.intro:
Two stones with two empty cells between them form a bridge: whichever cell the opponent takes, you take the other. A move that leaves two ways to connect wins.

A bridge is the strongest link in Hex — almost as good as touching.
ls.b_bridge.goal: Play the move that connects in two whatever happens.
ls.b_bridge.hint: Look for a cell that makes a bridge (or two possible finishing cells).
ls.b_bridge.why: {m} leaves two ways to connect: the opponent can stop only one.
ls.b_bridge.ng: After {x} the opponent can block. {m} leaves two ways.
ls.b_save.title: Saving the bridge
ls.b_save.intro:
The opponent has just played into one cell of your bridge. Take the other cell at once and the two stones stay connected.

An intrusion is often a test: if you look away, your chain is cut.
ls.b_save.hint: Find the bridge the opponent's last stone touches.
ls.b_save.why: {m} saves the bridge — your chain is still unbreakable.
ls.b_save.ng: After {x} your chain can be cut. {m} saves the bridge.
ls.b_edge.title: The edge template
ls.b_edge.intro:
A stone on the 2nd row from your edge, with the two cells below it empty, is already connected to the edge: if one cell is taken, take the other.

You don't need to play on the edge itself — that wastes a move.
ls.b_edge.goal: Play the move that wins (use the 2nd row).
ls.b_edge.hint: Look for a cell on the 2nd row from your edge with both edge cells below it empty.
ls.b_edge.why: {m} reaches your edge through the template.
ls.b_edge.ng: {x} is too slow. {m} uses the edge template.
ls.t_double.title: Double threats
ls.t_double.intro:
Strong Hex moves create two threats at once. If each threat is a bridge or an edge template, the opponent can stop at most one of them.

Count: how many stones does each of your ways still need? A move that keeps two short ways is the key.
ls.t_double.goal: Find the only move that connects within three moves.
ls.t_double.hint: The key stone links to two different groups or edges.
ls.t_double.why: {m} creates two threats; the opponent can stop only one.
ls.t_double.ng: After {x} the opponent has a defence. {m} was the double threat.
ls.t_stop.title: Stopping a double threat
ls.t_stop.intro:
When the opponent threatens to connect in two moves, blocking one way is not enough. Play where both threats pass — usually the single link that is not a bridge.

A bridge cannot be cut, so look for the opponent's weakest link.
ls.t_stop.goal: Stop the opponent from connecting within two moves.
ls.t_stop.hint: Find the opponent's weakest link — the gap that is not a bridge.
ls.t_stop.why: {m} cuts the threat at its weak point.
ls.t_stop.ng: After {x} the opponent still connects in two. {m} stops it.
ls.t_ladder.title: Ladders
ls.t_ladder.intro:
When a chain is blocked near the edge, it can push along the 2nd row while the opponent blocks on the 1st row: a ladder. The ladder wins if it reaches a stone of yours further along — a ladder escape.

Before you start a ladder, check that it ends at your escape, not at the opponent's edge.
ls.t_ladder.hint: Push the ladder towards your stone on the edge.
ls.t_ladder.why: {m} is the right way: the ladder reaches your escape.
ls.t_ladder.ng: {x} lets the opponent block. {m} wins the ladder.
ls.t_edge3.title: Edge template III
ls.t_edge3.intro:
A stone on the 3rd row is also connected to the edge if a small area below it is empty (the ziggurat). When the opponent intrudes, answer inside the template so that a bridge or a 2nd-row template remains.

The dots in the picture are the template area. The ringed cell is its key point.
ls.t_edge3.goal: Keep the connection to the edge.
ls.t_edge3.hint: Answer next to your stone, on the side the intrusion did not take.
ls.t_edge3.why: {m} keeps the template: you still reach the edge.
ls.t_edge3.ng: After {x} the connection to the edge can be cut. {m} keeps it.
ls.s_center.title: The strongest first moves
ls.s_center.sub: The centre and the short diagonal
ls.s_center.intro:
Without the swap rule, the first player opens in the centre or on the short diagonal (the line between the two obtuse corners): from there both red edges are close.

The values are the AI's winning chances. A move within a few percent of the best scores full points.
ls.s_center.hint: The best moves are near the centre of the board.
ls.s_swap.title: Should you swap?
ls.s_swap.intro:
With the swap rule, Blue decides after Red's first move: swap (take that stone) if it is strong, or play a normal move if it is weak. Moves near the centre are strong; moves on the border are usually weak.

Press the "Swap" button above the board to swap, or click a cell to play.
ls.s_swap.goal: Swap, or play the best move.
ls.s_swap.hint: How strong is Red's first stone? The first-move map in the openings shows it.
ls.s_block.title: Blocking at a distance
ls.s_block.sub: Don't stand right next to it
ls.s_block.intro:
A block right next to the opponent's stone is easy to go round with a bridge. Block further away, in front of its path, so your stone also builds your own connection.

Strong players often block two or three rows ahead.
ls.s_block.hint: Block in front of the opponent's stone, but not touching it.
ls.s_plan.title: Choosing a plan
ls.s_plan.intro:
In the middle game, look at both players' shortest connections. The best move usually helps your connection and blocks the opponent's at the same time.

The player cards show how many more cells each side needs.
ls.s_plan.hint: Look where both players' shortest paths cross.
pz.grpWinSub: Join your edges within N moves however the opponent defends (7×7 and 9×9).
pz.grpBlockSub: The opponent threatens a forced connection: find the only move that stops it.
pz.th.c3.sub: One move that makes two ways
op.grp.swap.sub: 11×11: the strong centre is swapped; balanced border openings are played on
op.grp.noswap.sub: 11×11: the centre opening and Blue's best answers
op.center11.short: The strongest move, so Blue swaps
op.center11.intro:
f6, the centre, is Red's strongest first move — so with the swap rule Blue takes it over.
Then Red plays as if it were Blue's game: it must block the swapped stone and build its own chain.
op.edge11a.intro:
A first move on the border is weak enough that Blue does not swap, yet not lost for Red.
This is the kind of opening strong players use with the swap rule.
op.edge11b.intro:
A second balanced border opening: Blue does not swap and answers in the centre area.
Watch how Red uses its border stone later in the game.
op.ring11.intro:
A first move on the 2nd row is a little stronger than the border but still close to even.
Blue does not swap here and fights for the centre.
op.f6r1.short: Blue's best answer to the centre
op.f6r1.intro:
Without the swap rule Red opens in the centre. These are the answers the AI found best for Blue.
Blue blocks Red's way to its edges while preparing its own chain.
op.f6r2.intro:
Another good answer to the centre opening (swap off).
The two sides race: every stone both blocks and connects.
op.f6r3.intro:
A third answer to the centre opening (swap off).
Compare the three lines: where does Blue block, and how does Red go round?
op.c7.intro:
On 7×7 the centre is a winning first move (in theory Red always wins from it).
A short line to see how quickly bridges reach the edges.
op.c9.intro:
On 9×9 the centre is again the strongest first move.
Blue must block at a distance, Red answers with bridges.
op.e9.intro:
On 9×9 with the swap rule, Red opens on the border so that Blue does not swap.
A good way to practise swap-rule openings on a small board.
